title: ASG launches a paper recycling project
body: ASG began a paper recycling programme, setting ecology trash cans at points across campus and later extending collection to cans and bottles. Money from the sale of recycled paper was ploughed back into the Environmental Committee's work, which was chaired by Joe Cheak.
note: The cited Herald 52:12, 6 Oct 1972 carries "Paper Recycling Project to be Launched by Associated Student Government" - an announcement of a future project, reported here as a completed launch. Every detail in the body (ecology trash cans, cans and bottles, money ploughed back, Joe Cheak) comes from the 1973 Talisman, which is not cited. Note also the cited issue is No. 12, not the unnumbered "6 Oct" label.

title: Jimmy Buffett plays a mini-concert
body: Jimmy Buffett came to campus on Thursday 19 April 1973 in levis and a cowboy shirt, carrying two Martin guitars, for an ASG mini-concert. The Herald had billed the show two days earlier.
note: The cited Herald 52:51, 17 Apr 1973 carries only the advance notice "Mini-Concert Set Thursday - Jimmy Buffett", which cannot support the levis, cowboy shirt, two Martin guitars, or that the show took place. All of that is in the 1973 Talisman ("On April 19, entertainer Jimmy Buffett... came to the Western campus dressed in levis and a cowboy shirt"), which is not cited. The cited headline also does not name ASG.

title: Edmund Muskie calls for Nixon's impeachment
body: ASG's lecture series brought Senator Edmund Muskie of Maine on 11 December 1973 to speak on 'The Restoration of Confidence'. Muskie called for the impeachment of President Nixon, saying he had decided after much soul-searching on the night of the Saturday Night Massacre that it was the only way to raise the issue.
note: The cited Herald 53:26, 4 Dec 1973 carries only "Sen. Edmund Muskie Lecture Set for Dec. 11" - an advance notice a week before the event. It cannot support the topic quotation, the impeachment call, or the Saturday Night Massacre remark. All of that, plus the ASG tie, is in the 1974 Talisman (topic "The Restoration of Confidence"; caption "In an ASG-sponsored lecture, Senator Edmund Muskie called for the impeachment of President Nixon"), which is not cited.

title: Sam Ervin analyses Watergate
body: Senator Sam Ervin, chairman of the Senate Watergate committee, spoke at Western on 2 April 1974 under the contract ASG had signed in February. The Talisman recorded that the 1973-74 lecture series ended with Ervin and with Representative John Conyers of Michigan, a member of the House Judiciary Committee who voted for impeachment.
note: Herald 53:50, 5 Apr 1974 does report the event ("Caudill, Tom. Sam Ervin Analyzes Watergate Situation"), and 53:48 has "Sam Ervin to Speak Tuesday" (Tuesday = 2 Apr). But nothing ties Ervin to ASG: the 1974 Talisman lists him only under "Other lecturers scheduled for 1974", alongside Vincent Price, in a passage about the University Lecture Series. The "contract ASG had signed in February" is unsupported. The claim that the Talisman recorded the series ending with Ervin and Rep. John Conyers is contradicted - Conyers does not appear anywhere in the 1974 Talisman (the only Conyers in its index is a student, Mary Anne Conyers); Conyers spoke, per Herald 29 Mar 1974, but with no ASG or series attribution.

title: ASG books its fall entertainment fare
body: The Herald reported that ASG had booked its fall entertainment. The season it announced ran from the August bluegrass festival through the Doc Severinsen Homecoming concert, the America free concert and the Kiss date in December.
note: The headline is real - Herald Vol. 50 No. 2, 30 Aug 1974: "Associated Student Government Books Fall Entertainment Fare". But the body's description of what was announced is impossible: the 1975 Talisman states that ASG booked Al Stewart for 3 November, that Stewart's US tour was then cancelled over immigration law, and that only then did "LaCivita book Kiss... in the place of Al Stewart". Kiss cannot have been on a slate announced on 30 August 1974.

title: The Bar-Kays break even
body: ASG presented the Bar-Kays, the backing band on Isaac Hayes's 'Hot Buttered Soul' and 'Shaft', in one of its major mini-concerts on 25 October 1974. The seven-piece group held a distinction among campus concerts that year: ASG broke even on it.
note: The cited Herald Vol. 50 No. 17, 25 Oct 1974 carries only "Tewell, Terry. Bar-Kays to Perform in Mini-Concert Tonight" - an advance notice, which gives no financial result. The substance, including the money claim, is in the uncited 1975 Talisman: "ASG presented the Bar-Kays in one of its major mini-concerts of the year... The seven-member group held another distinction among campus concerts - ASG broke even on the Bar-Kays concert."

title: Pure Prairie League plays two shows, the first ruined by the sound
body: ASG billed Pure Prairie League for two shows in Van Meter on 31 January 1975. Sound problems ruined most of the first set at 7:30 and bassist Mike Reilly asked the 9:30 audience whether anyone had seen the first show; the problems were fixed and the second show was first-rate.
note: The cited Herald Vol. 50 No. 31, 24 Jan 1975 carries only "Associated Student Government Bills Pure Prairie League" - an advance notice a week before the show. The whole review is in the uncited 1975 Talisman: "bassist Mike Rieley... asked the audience of the 9:30 concert on Jan. 31... The 7:30 show was not as bad as Rieley said - it was worse. Sound problems ruined most of the first act... All sound problems were solved, however, before the second show, which was first-rate." (A Talisman caption elsewhere misdates the same concert to October 30.)

title: Charles Berlitz opens the ASG lecture series on the Bermuda Triangle
body: Charles Berlitz, author of 'The Bermuda Triangle', opened the ASG lecture series in Van Meter on 9 September 1975 to a standing-room-only audience. He told them that since 1945 more than 100 planes and ships and 1,000 people had vanished in the region, and ran through theories from magnetisation to alien beings.
note: The cited Herald 51:4, 9 Sep 1975 carries "Hoodoo Sea to Be Subject of Associated Student Government Lecture - Charles Berlitz, Bermuda Triangle" - a same-day advance notice ('to be subject of'), which cannot report a standing-room-only audience or the content. All of it is in the uncited 1976 Talisman: "shadows lent an eerie atmosphere to the standing-room-only audience... Charles Berlitz... opened the Associated Student Government (ASG) lecture series... In the Sept. 9 lecture... Since 1945, more than 100 planes and ships and 1,000 people have vanished", with the magnetisation and alien-beings theories.

title: Linda Ronstadt makes ASG $4,300
body: Approximately 6,500 filled Diddle Arena for Linda Ronstadt on Saturday 1 November 1975, with Goose Creek Symphony and Andrew Gold on the bill. The Homecoming concert netted a profit of $4,300 for ASG, and Rick Kelley and president Steve Henry called it one of the most successful in years; its success guaranteed the free Spinners concert that January.
note: The cited Herald 51:19, 31 Oct 1975 is the pre-Homecoming issue; its only relevant item is "Linda Ronstadt Heads Concert Bill" - an advance notice that cannot contain a 1 November attendance figure or a profit. Everything is in the uncited 1976 Talisman: "Approximately 6,500 attended the concert on Saturday, Nov. 1. The Homecoming concert netted a profit of $4,300 for the ASG. Kelley and ASG President Steve Henry said the concert was one of the most successful in years. So successful, in fact, that it guaranteed another free concert (The Spinners and Wet Willie) on Jan. 30", with Goose Creek Symphony and Andrew Gold also named.

title: Natalie Cole sings to 325 in Van Meter
body: ASG sponsored the jazz vocalist Natalie Cole in Van Meter on 10 December 1975 before an estimated crowd of 325. The late Nat King Cole's daughter sang 'This Will Be', 'Killing Me Softly With His Song', 'Honky Tonk Women' and 'You Are the Sunshine of My Life'.
note: The cited Herald 51:29, 9 Dec 1975 carries "Associated Student Government to Sponsor Jazz Vocalist" - an advance notice the day before, which establishes ASG sponsorship but cannot give the crowd of 325 or the setlist. Those are in the uncited 1976 Talisman: "On Dec. 10, jazz vocalist Natalie Cole also performed in Van Meter to an estimated crowd of 325", with 'Killing Me Softly', 'Honky Tonk Women', 'You Are the Sunshine of My Life' and 'This Will Be'.

title: Andrae Crouch and the Disciples in the Garrett ballroom
body: The soul gospel group Andrae Crouch and the Disciples performed in the Garrett Conference Center ballroom on 8 February 1976. The Talisman lists it among the year's ASG entertainment alongside the free concerts.
note: The 1976 Talisman does say "Gospel group Andrae Crouch and the Disciples, a soul gospel group, performed in the Garrett Conference Center ballroom on Feb. 8" - but it does not tie the show to ASG in any way. The entry's assertion that "The Talisman lists it among the year's ASG entertainment alongside the free concerts" overstates what the source does: it is an on-campus event with no student-government attribution.

title: Harrison Salisbury lectures
body: The Pulitzer Prize-winning newspaper columnist Harrison Salisbury lectured on the evening of 30 March 1976. He was one of the spring speakers scheduled by ASG's lecture committee.
note: The cited Herald 51:50, 30 Mar 1976 carries "Journalist to Lecture Tonight - Harrison Salisbury" - a same-day advance notice. The 1976 Talisman likewise only says he was among "Other lecturers scheduled in the spring... Harrison Salisbury on March 30 and author Truman Capote on April 21." Nothing I could reach reports that the lecture actually took place.

title: James Taylor closes the year with a free concert
body: James Taylor played a free concert on Friday 23 April 1976, with Henry Gross also on the bill. The Herald reported the following week that the James Taylor and Henry Gross concerts had been a big success.
note: The cited Herald 51:56, 20 Apr 1976 carries only "James Taylor to Play in Free Concert Friday", and 51:57 has "James Taylor Performance Will Be Tonight" - both advance notices. Neither names Henry Gross or ASG, and neither can support that the concert happened or the follow-up 'big success' report. The 1976 Talisman only says "James Taylor was scheduled to present a free concert in April."

title: Jimmy Buffett and the Coral Reefer Band close the year
body: Jimmy Buffett and the Coral Reefer Band were set for Diddle Arena on 27 April 1977. The set drew on 'Changes in Latitudes, Changes in Attitudes', 'Livin' and Dyin' in 3/4 Time', 'A-1-A' and 'Havana Daydreamin''.
note: The cited Herald 52:47, 25 Mar 1977 carries only "Jimmy Buffett Concert Set for April 27" - an advance notice five weeks ahead, which cannot support the setlist. That is in the uncited 1977 Talisman: "Jimmy Buffett and the Coral Reefer Band appeared at Diddle Arena April 27. Highlights... included selections from 'Changes in Latitudes, Changes in Attitudes,' as well as tunes from the albums, 'Livin' and Dyin' in 3/4 Time,' 'A-1-A,' and 'Havana Daydreamin'.'" Neither source ties the show to ASG.

title: Homecoming concert booked without a signed contract
body: A week before the Homecoming show the Herald reported that Western had never signed a contract with Sunshine Promotions, the firm that had booked Player and Exile for 3 November. Sunshine refused to sign because the university demanded a $100,000 performance bond guaranteeing that all bills would be paid; the company said Indiana insurers wanted 100 percent collateral and a $2,000 service fee for it. The Homecoming concert went ahead on an oral agreement alone.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 19, 26 October 1978

note: Herald 10-26-1978, Vol. 54 No. 19 confirmed. The front-page story 'Concert contract hasn't been signed' supports the core: Western has not signed with Sunshine because the firm won't post a $100,000 bond required by the university; the bond would guarantee all bills related to the three concerts would be paid; Player and Exile booked for a Nov. 3 concert; Sybesma cites '100 percent collateral and $2,000 service fee insurance companies say they must have.' TWO PROBLEMS. (1) The closing sentence, 'The Homecoming concert went ahead on an oral agreement alone,' cannot come from this issue - the concert was still eight days in the future. I read the full continuation on p.3; there is no mention of an oral or verbal agreement anywhere in the issue. That wording appears in the 9 November editorial (record 3429), which says the show was 'booked and produced on an emergency basis with only an [oral] agreement between Sunshine and the university.' Cite that issue instead. (2) 'Indiana insurers' is not in this source, which says only 'insurance companies'; the Indiana detail comes from Talisman 1979. Also 'Sunshine refused to sign' overstates it - the article says the firm won't post the bond, and Sybesma said his company might agree to put up money before each concert.

title: Dick Gregory draws about 400
body: Civil rights activist Dick Gregory gave a free afternoon lecture in the Center Theater as part of the Black Awareness Symposium, opening with comic lines before turning on United States actions in Vietnam, the Middle East, Iran and Jonestown. About 400 came, against 36 for the Reverend Arthur Langford's "Martin Luther King Jr.: A Portrait" in February. That evening the Heritage Hall Jazz Band from New Orleans played to a half-filled Van Meter Auditorium.
note: The facts all check out but the source never ties the event to student government. Talisman 1979 pp.38-39 confirms: free afternoon lecture by Gregory in Center Theater; comic opening then criticism of US actions in 'Vietnam, the Middle East, Iran and Jonestown, Guyana'; Nemeth quoted 'The King portrayal drew only 36 people, but about 400 people showed up to hear Dick Gregory'; Langford's 'Martin Luther King Jr.: A Portrait' on Feb. 14 attracted 36; Heritage Hall Jazz Band from New Orleans in a half-filled Van Meter on March 22. But the Black Awareness Symposium section attributes the programme entirely to Tim Nemeth and the university, and the Talisman's own University Center Board section (p.82) lists 'Martin Luther King Jr.: A Portrait' and 'the Heritage Hall Jazz Band' as CENTER BOARD lectures-and-concerts programmes, not ASG ones. If you want the ASG tie for Gregory, it is in the 18 January 1979 Herald ('ASG signs 3 lectures'), which should be cited alongside. Two smaller points: the source does not say the jazz band played 'that evening', only that Gregory spoke 'earlier that day'; and it dates Langford to Feb. 14, which your 'in February' covers.

title: Gerard O'Neill on space colonies
body: Gerard O'Neill, a physics professor at Princeton and author of "The High Frontier," told 100 people in the Center Theater that space colonies and orbiting solar power stations were possible with existing technology and could relieve the energy crisis. He said President Carter had abolished the NASA office exploring space colonisation while signing a bill to develop a particle beam weapon for use in space. ASG had signed him for $2,000 and the lecture was free.
note: The lecture content checks out but the money and the ASG attribution do not come from the cited source. Talisman 1979 Lectures section (p.97) confirms: O'Neill, Princeton physics professor, author of 'The High Frontier'; 'said in his April 2 lecture that space colonies and solar power stations are possible with current technology'; 'The 100 people in the Center Theater'; Carter 'had abolished a National Aeronautics and Space Administration office that was exploring space colonization'; Carter 'signed a bill for the development of a particle beam weapon... to be placed in space.' But the Lectures section names no sponsor and gives no fee - I read the whole section (Jarvis, Bethge, Goldberg, Koop, O'Neill) and ASG is never mentioned and no speaker fee appears anywhere. 'ASG had signed him for $2,000 and the lecture was free' is sourced from the 18 January 1979 Herald instead; cite that for the money.

title: Shirley Chisholm closes the Black Awareness Symposium
body: Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm had been booked for Black Awareness Week in February but cancelled all her appearances for that month, which is why the week was stretched into a semester-long symposium. Her rescheduled free lecture filled Van Meter Auditorium at 8 p.m. on 18 April with a crowd of about 250, predominantly black, who shouted and chanted in response. She said she was a people's politician who could not be manipulated and was there "to teach and to tell people what they don't like to hear."
note: Several specifics are absent from the cited source and one is internally contradicted. Talisman 1979 pp.38-39 supports: Chisholm was rescheduled to April 18 after cancelling her February lecture, which is why Black Awareness Week became a semester-long symposium; 'The crowd of about 250, predominantly black, shouted and chanted in response'; she is 'a people's politician' who 'cannot be manipulated'; 'here to teach and to tell people what they don't like to hear.' NOT in the source: the venue (Van Meter), the 8 p.m. start, that the lecture was free, and 'filled Van Meter Auditorium' - the same yearbook states on p.79 that Van Meter 'holds slightly more than 1,000,' so 250 people cannot have filled it. Also 'cancelled all her appearances for that month' is the 18 January Herald's wording, not the Talisman's, which says only that she 'canceled her February lecture.' And as with the other lecture entries, the cited section makes no ASG connection.

title: Randy Crawford and the Crusaders play free to 1,409
body: The jazz group The Crusaders, with Randy Crawford opening, played Diddle Arena free to full-time students on 26 April. Turnstiles registered 1,409 people at the intermission, of whom only about 1,200 were students, less than 10 percent of the student body, and an estimated 200 tickets sold to non-students brought in about $1,000. The university paid $11,396 in expenses, including $6,000 for The Crusaders and $1,000 for Crawford, and assistant university centers director Tim Nemeth said afterwards, "More than likely, that's the last free show you'll see."
money: $11,396 in expenses; $6,000 to The Crusaders, $1,000 to Randy Crawford; about $1,000 taken at the gate

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 59, 1 May 1979

note: Every figure is exact, but the source explicitly attributes the show to the university rather than to student government. Herald 5-1-1979, Vol. 54 No. 59, '1,409 attend Crusaders' concert': Thursday concert in Diddle Arena, free for full-time students; '1,409 people had been registered by the turnstiles... at the intermission'; 'Only 1,200 students - less than 10 percent of the student population - attended'; 'An estimated 200 tickets were sold to non-students, bringing in about $1,000'; 'the university paid about $11,396 in expenses for the concert, including $6,000 for The Crusaders and $1,000 for Ms. Crawford'; and the Nemeth quote 'More than likely, that's the last free show you'll see.' ASG appears nowhere in the article, and Nemeth is quoted saying 'the university, not Sunshine Promotions, handled all the expenses involved.' Talisman 1979 p.79 likewise files it under concerts Western sponsored 'independent of Sunshine Promotions.' Keep it only if the archive covers university-run shows, and reword to drop any implied ASG credit.

title: ASG's International Week
body: ASG ran International Week nightly in the university center in November 1980, with two or three countries featured each evening through films, lectures, folk dances and slides given by students and faculty from those countries. Programme chairman Osama Shariff opened the week with a talk on Palestine and a Red Cross film on Palestinian children, and the week closed on a presentation of Brazil and Colombia. Nine countries were covered in all: Switzerland, Palestine, Iceland, Malaysia, Colombia, Brazil, India, Pakistan and France.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 56, No. 22, 13 November 1980

note: The cited Herald supports the sponsorship and the opening night but not the two most specific claims. Herald 11-13-1980, Vol. 56 No. 22, 'ASG sponsors international affair': International Week 'sponsored by Associated Student Government'; 'The nightly event, which began Monday, ends with a final presentation on Brazil and Colombia at 7 tonight'; two or three countries each night using 'films, lectures, folk dances and slides'; students and faculty from those countries presenting; 'Program chairman Osama Shariff opened the activities Monday,' gave a talk on Palestine and showed 'a Red Cross film on how Palestinian children survive.' NOT in this issue: the nine-country list (Switzerland, Iceland, Malaysia, India, Pakistan, France are never named - I searched the full issue text) and the university-center venue. Both of those come from Talisman 1981 ('A year of resolutions'), which says 'Osama Sharif... coordinated the nightly programs in the university center. Nine countries - Switzerland, Palestine, Iceland, Malaysia, Colombia, Brazil, India, Pakistan and France - were featured.' Add that second citation and the entry stands.

title: The discount cards finally arrive
body: The ASG-endorsed discount cards reached campus, though the organisation still did not know how many it had or exactly what was on them. Distribution was held back while ASG worked out what the contracts, valid from 1 September 1981 to 1 September 1982, actually promised the merchants. Six businesses had been identified as buying space, though Steve Fuller thought at least fifteen had signed.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 57, No. 11, 1 October 1981

note: Herald 10-1-1981, Vol. 57 No. 11, 'Discount cards here, but won't go out yet' contradicts two claims. (1) The source says ASG 'still doesn't know HOW the 14,000 cards... WILL BE DISTRIBUTED' - the uncertainty is about distribution logistics, not the quantity or contents. The article states the count (14,000) and the contents plainly: 'The cards offer discounts to students from 21 listed merchants.' So 'did not know how many it had or exactly what was on them' misreads the sentence. (2) The reason distribution was held back is given as Bush being 'busy with other projects,' handing it to the communications committee, whose chairwoman Laura Simms 'is still working on a plan' - nothing about working out what the contracts promised merchants. (3) The 'six businesses... at least fifteen had signed' figures are not in this issue at all; they are in the 29 September issue (record 2412), and they sit oddly beside this issue's 21 listed merchants. What this issue does support: the cards 'have finally arrived,' were delivered the previous day, and were 'valid until Sept. 1, 1982.'

title: Complaints about the turnout for the New Christy Minstrels
body: A letter from Dan Gritton in the last Herald of the year criticised attendance at the New Christy Minstrels show, the earliest recorded grumble about an empty house at a campus concert.
note: The letter is real: "Gritton, Dan. Criticizes Attendance at New Christy Minstrels Show" (and a second, "Hayden, Phyllis. Timing Hurt New Christy Minstrels Show"). But nothing in the source ties the concert to Associated Students, and "earliest recorded grumble" is an unsourced superlative. Filed as a concert entry on an unattributed campus show.

title: Planning ahead to boost activities
body: Gary Hunt reported for the Herald that the Associated Student Government was planning ahead to boost campus activities. The article ran in the second week of William Menser's year as the government's first student regent.
note: The article is verified ("Hunt, Gary. Associated Student Government Planning Ahead to Boost Activities"). But Menser was the Associated Students president, elected in the landslide reported in 46:20, not a student regent. Herald 47:10 (2 Nov 1967) still runs "Henry Ward Favors Student on Board of Regents," i.e. the student-regent seat was an open campaign question at the time, not a post Menser held.

title: A mock election for governor, preceded by debates
body: The Herald announced a gubernatorial mock election on campus for the following Tuesday, to be preceded by debates. The result ran a week later: Western's voters gave Louie Nunn an easy victory over Henry Ward, matching the state result.
note: "Gubernatorial Mock Election Slated Tuesday After Debates" (47:7) and the result "WKU Voters Give Nunn Easy Victory Ward" (47:10) both check out. But no source ties the mock election to the student government, and the entry's date is the announcement issue: balloting was the following Tuesday, 31 October.

title: The Lettermen added to the Homecoming entertainment bill
body: Dave West reported for the Herald that the Lettermen would add class to the entertainment bill for Homecoming week 1967. The issue also covered the Homecoming queen candidates and the week's schedule.
note: "West, Dave. Lettermen Add Class to Entertainment Bill" is in 47:7. But nothing ties the booking to student government, and Herald 47:5 (12 Oct) had already run "Lettermen to Perform Tuesday," pointing to a 17 October performance rather than Homecoming week.

title: Wilson Pickett headlines a soul concert
body: The Herald's front page for 14 December 1967 announced a soul concert that night starring Wilson Pickett. It is the biggest single act the record shows on campus in Menser's year.
note: "Soul Concert Tonight Stars Wilson Pickett" is in 47:15 for 14 December, so the date holds. But the source gives no sponsor, so nothing connects the concert to Associated Students, and front-page placement plus "biggest single act" are not shown by an article index.

title: The Association opens the Associated Students year
body: The Herald announced that a concert by the Association would open the Associated Students entertainment year. Photographs of the concert ran in the issue of 24 October.
note: 48:4 has "'Association' Concert Billed to Open Associated Students Year" — a billing, not a held concert, and it gives no date. The entry files it as a concert on 10 October, which is only the issue date. The 24 October photographs are in an issue that is not cited.

title: A presidential mock election on campus
body: The Herald announced campus mock election balloting for the following Monday and argued in an editorial that the vote would reveal how aware students were. The result appeared a week later: Richard Nixon and Marlow Cook carried Western.
note: "Campus Mock Election Balloting Set Monday" and the editorial "Mock Election to Reveal Awareness" are in 48:5. But balloting was Monday 21 October, not the 17th; the Nixon and Cook result is in an uncited issue; and no source ties the election to student government.

title: The Broadway musical '1776' staged for Homecoming
body: The Herald announced that the curtain would rise on "1776" the next day, and Jeanne Jackson called it Western's best ever musical in the Homecoming issue. John Lyne's own account of his year listed the co-sponsorship of "1776" as an example of the government's move from entertainment to a wider cultural programme.
note: "Curtain Rises Tomorrow for '1776' Performance" (50:11) and "Tickets for '1776' Available Tuesday" (50:6) support a 7 October curtain. Everything tying it to student government fails: Jeanne Jackson's "best ever musical" is in neither cited index, and the 1971 Talisman contains no Lyne account of his year — only a caption, "The writing of the Declaration of Independence was portrayed through the wit and music of the cast of '1776,'" with no sponsor named.

title: Pacific Gas and Electric flops at Homecoming
body: Ernie Hearion's review in the Herald was headed "Utilities Down Sharply on Entertainment Market." The 1971 Talisman was blunter, writing that Pacific Gas and Electric turned on very few when they appeared as part of Homecoming weekend.
note: Both quotations are genuine: Hearion's "Utilities Down Sharply on Entertainment Market" (50:13) and the Talisman's "Utilities stocks went down as Pacific Gas and Electric 'turned on' very few when they appeared as part of Homecoming weekend." But the yearbook places the concert in Homecoming weekend, which the same 50:13 issue recaps as already past; 13 October 1970 was a Tuesday and is the review's publication date, not the concert date.

title: Lyne's account: entertainment becomes a cultural programme
body: In his signed statement in the 1971 Talisman, president John Lyne wrote that the entertainment side of the government's work had been expanded into a cultural programmes concept, that big-name concerts continued but names outside the top forty such as Ravi Shankar had been brought in, and that theatrical events had been sponsored including the co-sponsorship of "1776." He also recorded that a student-run lecture series had been added that year, that the student discount programme with local merchants had been maintained, and that the government was working towards a legal service for students including a legal defence fund and a student advocates' corps.
note: The 1971 Talisman contains no signed statement by Lyne. The Lyne material is an interview profile running roughly pp. 80-85, not p. 66, and it does not contain the listed content. Repeated full-text searches show the volume has no instance of "discount," "legal," "advocate," "forty," or "cultural programs." Only unattributed captions for Ravi Shankar and "1776" exist, and the lecture series is named as "The University Lecture Series," not a student-run one.

title: The Emme Kemp Jazz Trio opens the mini-concert season
body: The Herald of 31 August announced that the Kemp Trio had set a concert. The 1972 Talisman records the Emme Kemp Jazz Trio as the first of several small-scale concerts staged that autumn, the format the Associated Students adopted to give students better quality entertainment at lower cost.
note: Both halves of the sourcing are real — Herald 51:2 has "Kemp Trio Sets Concert" and the 1972 Talisman has "The Emme Kemp Jazz Trio presented the first of several small scale concerts staged during the fall semester" — but neither gives 2 September or any other date, so the entry's date is unsupported.

title: Isaac Hayes plays the rescheduled date
body: The 1972 Talisman records that the concert cancelled in February was rescheduled by the Associated Students for 23 March. Stephanie Madison's review in the Herald of 28 March, "No Introductions Necessary as Isaac Hayes Movement Speaks to the People," confirms the show went ahead.
note: Madison's review "No Introductions Necessary as Isaac Hayes Movement Speaks to the People" (51:44) does show the concert went ahead. But the cited yearbook says only that Hayes "later contacted Western to reschedule his performance in March" — it does not give 23 March, and no source consulted supplies that date.

title: Reginald Glass on block-booking and the price of entertainment
body: Reginald Glass, the first black vice president of the Associated Students, headed the activities committee and co-ordinated student cultural activities, signing the contracts for concerts and speakers. In the 1972 Talisman he said he had wanted to do something about the high prices of entertainment but found it hard to reduce them because block-booking with schools in Kentucky and Tennessee was difficult to arrange, and that he had hoped to bring in different types of groups so most student factions would be satisfied at some point in the year.
note: Only a caption is confirmed: "Reginald Glass, vice-president of Associated Students, is signing contracts." The quoted views — wanting to do something about high prices, block-booking with Kentucky and Tennessee schools being hard to arrange, hoping to satisfy most student factions — are not in the 1972 Talisman text; "block booking" and "high prices" return no match. Herald 51:53 does carry "Moore, Chris. Black Vice-President Finds Race is No Problem – Reginald Glass," but that issue is not the cited source.

title: The year's programme summed up in the yearbook
body: The 1972 Talisman summarised Linda Jones's year under the heading "A.S. makes great strides in implementing new programs": in entertainment, mini-concerts, a coffee house in West Hall and the Gaslight film series joined several top-name musical groups and lecturers. It also recorded that the Associated Students conducted the elections for class officers, Who's Who and Homecoming queen, held the October mock election for governor, ran a symposium at which students could question administrators, sponsored the Homecoming dance, and revived the Kentucky Student Association among the state's student governments.
note: The heading "A.S. makes great strides in implementing new programs" does not appear in the 1972 Talisman, nor do "Gaslight," "Cellar," "West Hall" or "coffee house." The volume does mention Who's Who, a Homecoming queen and a Kentucky Student Association convention, but in unrelated passages, not as an itemised summary of what Associated Students ran. The p. 272 summary as described is not in the source.

title: ASG president assassinated in a members-only killing game
body: ASG members spent the autumn playing an assassination game with toy guns, and president Tim Todd was shot at about 8 p.m. on 2 October in his State Street apartment while wearing only a bathrobe, fresh out of the shower. Kathryn Michelsen, who killed Todd and three other congress members the same night, led the field in kills until Gamaliel freshman Janet Dyer shot her between the eyes near the university center. Dyer killed three more people that Sunday, two of them in front of their girlfriends.
note: Herald 62:13, 9 Oct 1986, "ASG members all wet from playing with guns." Most of the entry checks out: Tim Todd "was assassinated last Thursday at about 8 p.m. wearing only a bathrobe in his State Street apartment" (9 Oct issue, so 2 Oct - date correct); the game was ASG's, "sponsored by the Public Relations Committee"; Michelsen led in kills "until Gamaliel freshman Janet Dyer shot her" "right between the eyes" near the university center. BUT the Sunday kills are misattributed. The source: "Michelsen killed three other congress members the same night she shot Todd, including a sleeping Holger Velastegui. Sunday night SHE killed three people, two of whom were slain in front of their girlfriends." That is Michelsen, not Dyer - and Dyer did not shoot Michelsen until "last night" (Wed 8 Oct), after that Sunday. The entry's final sentence must be rewritten. Minor: the weapons are squirt/water guns, not generic "toy guns."

title: ASG hosts the second statewide student government conference
body: ASG played host to the second annual statewide student government conference from Friday 27 March to Sunday 29 March at the American Plaza on Scottsville Road, with registration at $18 and open to all students. President Tim Todd expected about 50 student leaders, down from about 65 at the first conference, which ASG had also hosted, and said hosting would cost between $400 and $500. Saturday seminars covered leadership, communication and financial aid, with the Council on Higher Education flying in a financial aid consultant from Washington and sending its director, Gary S. Cox.
note: REJECT - announcement written up as a completed event. Herald 62:48, 26 Mar 1987 is headlined "Student government conference TO BE HELD Friday through Sunday" and reads "Western's Associated Student Government WILL BE HOST to the second annual statewide student government conference tomorrow through Sunday." Nothing in this issue reports that the conference took place; a follow-up issue would be needed. Everything else in the entry does match the source, including the figure I initially misread from OCR: the page image plainly reads "About 65 went to last year's conference, also hosted by ASG" - so the entry's "about 65" is correct. Also confirmed: about 50 expected, American Plaza on Scottsville Road, President Tim Todd, "Registration is $18", "Hosting the conference will cost between $400 and $500", CHE flying in a financial aid consultant from Washington D.C., and director D. Gary S. Cox attending. Fix the tense and the dating and this becomes usable.

title: Mock presidential election with the College Republicans
body: ASG co-sponsored a mock presidential election with the College Republicans on Tuesday 25 October, from 10:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. in the university center, with student identification cards required to vote. Public relations vice president Amos Gott said the aim was to see how Western felt as a community compared with Bowling Green and the national responses to the candidates, and expected a turnout at least as large as a student government election because everybody knew the candidates. Results were posted the next day on the glassed-in student government bulletin board in the university center.
note: REJECT - announcement written up as a completed event. Herald 64:17, 20 Oct 1988 is headlined "Mock election SCHEDULED; ASG hotline established" and reads "Associated Student Government is co-sponsoring a mock election with the College Republicans TUESDAY from 10:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. in the university center" - a Thursday paper describing the following Tuesday. The results line is future tense too: "The results WILL BE POSTED Wednesday in the glassed-in student government bulletin board in the university center, Gott said." The source therefore does not establish that the election happened, that anyone voted, or what the turnout was. The co-sponsorship, the times, the ID requirement, Amos Gott's stated purpose and his turnout expectation all match; only the tense and the dating are wrong.

title: An ASG hotline opens on Wednesday afternoons
body: Student government established a hotline so students could phone in complaints and suggestions, staffed by the ASG secretary from 1 to 4 p.m. every Wednesday from 26 October on the office line, 745-4354. Anything the secretary could not answer was referred to an executive officer. Administrative vice president Adrian Smoot said students could already call any time but did not, and that setting a fixed hour made people more likely to ring.
note: Same article (Herald 64:17, 20 Oct 1988). The hotline facts are all correct: "Students can voice their opinions by calling the student government office at 745-4354 between 1 and 4 p.m. every Wednesday starting next Wednesday" (i.e. 26 Oct); "Student government's secretary will answer the hotline and take complaints and suggestions about the organization, Gott said. Any questions she can not answer will be referred to an executive officer." BUT THE QUOTE IS ATTRIBUTED TO THE WRONG OFFICER. The source reads: "Students can call anytime during the week, but they don't, GOTT said. But if a time is set, HE said 'people are more apt to call than just any day.'" That is Amos Gott, public relations vice president. Adrian Smoot, administrative vice president, is quoted elsewhere on the page - "We're doing well without one, but we could do better with one" - and that is about the vacant parliamentarian post, not the hotline. Verified on the page image. Reattribute to Gott and this entry is fine; note also that 26 Oct is a prospective start date in a 20 Oct paper.

title: Coach for a Game puts a student on the bench with Ralph Willard
body: ASG created Coach for a Game as a spring counterpart to the fall's President for a Day, selling raffle tickets at 50 cents each with every member required to sell ten and the proceeds going to a philanthropic cause. Members sold from tables at Downing University Center and in DUC 119 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on 24 and 25 February, and the draw was held at the ASG meeting on 25 February. The winner served as Coach Ralph Willard's new assistant at the men's basketball game against Central Florida on 29 February, and public relations vice president Mistianna Holcomb, who wrote the bill, said it would become an annual event.
money: raffle tickets 50 cents each, ten per member

src.label: SGA Records, Bill 92-03-S, Establishment of a Coach for a Game Program

note: REJECT - the cited document supports almost none of the entry. Bill 92-03-S (verified on the page image) is UNDATED: the "INTRODUCED:" line is blank and First Reading, Second Reading, Pass, Fail and Other are all blank, so it cannot support a 1992-02-29 date or any date. It contains only: the purpose "To establish a Coach for a Game program"; "In the fall, ASG does sponsor President for a Day"; "it should be mandatory for each ASG member to sell ten tickets for this project at $.50 per ticket"; "The proceeds from this event will go towards a philanthropic cause"; AUTHOR: Mistianna Holcomb; SPONSOR: Public Relations. It says NOTHING about Ralph Willard, the Central Florida game, 29 February, the DUC and DUC 119 ticket tables on 24-25 February, the 10 a.m.-2 p.m. hours, the 25 February drawing, Holcomb's job title, or her saying it would become annual. Those all need a separate citation (minutes or a Herald story) or must be cut.

title: Project Western Week and the Don't Trash The Spirit clean-up
body: SGA ran Project Western Week from Monday 8 February, its biggest event a mass campus clean-up on Wednesday 10 February under the motto Don't Trash The Spirit. Students gathered with bin bags at about 3:30 p.m. at the New Co-Ed and New Sorority dorms, spread out across the width of campus and finished at Cherry Hall, and about 600 people were expected. The campus was divided into 23 sections taken by organisations that had signed up by 5 February and that stayed responsible for their areas until the end of term, with the group keeping the cleanest area to receive $500 from SGA.
money: $500 prize to the organisation with the cleanest area
note: REJECT for the 10 February clean-up specifically - it is announced, not reported. Herald 68:35, 9 Feb 1993, p.6, "SGA news: Students arm themselves with trash bags to clean up campus" opens "DON'T BE SURPRISED TOMORROW to see a mass of students, armed with trash bags, marching up the Hill." This page had no OCR layer, so I read it as an image. Everything else matches exactly: motto "Don't Trash The Spirit"; "The event will be the biggest part of Project Western Week, said Student Government Association President Joe Rains. Project Western Week began Monday and lasts through the week"; "Students will begin picking up trash around 3:30 p.m. at the New Co-Ed and New Sorority dorms. The group will spread out the width of the campus, and conclude their march at Cherry Hall"; "About 600 people are expected to attend"; "The campus will be divided into 23 sections"; "organizations had until Feb. 5 to sign up"; responsible "until the end of the semester"; "the group with the cleanest area gets $500 from SGA." The $500 is genuinely in the source. Only the past tense on the 10 Feb clean-up needs fixing; the 8 Feb start of the week is properly supported.

title: Weekend in the Woods runs again on 23 and 24 October
body: President Donald Smith told congress on 12 October 1993 that Weekend in the Woods would be held on 23 and 24 October. The leadership retreat, which ASG had been running since the early 1980s, was still on the organisation's calendar a decade after the fourth annual weekend recorded in the 1987 Talisman.
note: REJECT as dated - the source records only the announcement. SGA minutes, 12 Oct 1993: President Donald Smith "also informed member of Weekend in the Woods on October 23-24." That single line is all there is. The minutes do not show the retreat took place, who went, where, or what it cost, so an entry dated 1993-10-23 with a title asserting it "runs again" overstates the record. The body text is honest about this, so the fix is small: redate to the 12 Oct meeting and retitle as an announcement, or cite the minutes of a later meeting. Also note the added claim that ASG "had been running [it] since the early 1980s" is an inference from the 1987 Talisman's "fourth annual," not something either source states.

title: Warren County judge-executive candidates come to congress
body: Administrative vice president Scott Sivley announced on 12 October 1993 that the Warren County judge-executive candidates, Miller and Buchanon, would be guests at the congress meeting of 26 October. The invitation was part of a run of outside speakers SGA brought before its own meetings that autumn, alongside Head Start and the state legislators questioned earlier in the term.
note: REJECT as dated - announcement only. SGA minutes, 12 Oct 1993: Administrative Vice-President Sivley "announced that Warren County Judge Executive Candidates Miller and Buchanon WILL BE guests at the October 26." There is no record here that they appeared. Separately, the entry's closing clause - "alongside Head Start and the state legislators questioned earlier in the term" - is unsupported: the Head Start speakers are in these minutes, but nothing about state legislators being questioned earlier in the term appears anywhere in this document. Cut that or cite it.

title: $2,250 of organizational aid split between thirteen groups
body: Bill 94-2-S disbursed the $2,250 budgeted for organizational aid, after the committee spent more than four hours across three meetings deciding between applicants. Alpha Phi Omega, Campus Crusade for Christ and Delta Sigma Theta took $250 each, Beta Alpha Psi $200, the Topperettes $350, and the Association of Resident Assistants, Fellowship of Christian Athletes, International Club, Legion of Veterans, Phi Beta Sigma, SOTA, Students' Right to Life and United Student Activists shared the rest in grants of $100 to $150. It passed on 8 March 1994.

src.label: SGA Records, Bill 94-2-S, Organizational Aid Recipients

note: Bill 94-2-S. The frame is right - "First Reading 03-01-94 / Second Reading 03-08-94" stamped PASSED; "INTRODUCED: March 1, 1994"; "to disperse the $2,250.00 budgeted for Organizational Aid"; "The Organizational Aid Committee has spent over four hours in three meetings"; thirteen recipients. BUT TWO AMOUNTS ARE SWAPPED. I read the bill as a page image to be certain. The schedule is: Alpha Phi Omega $250, Association of Resident Assistants $125, Beta Alpha Psi $200, Campus Crusade for Christ $250, Delta Sigma Theta Sorority $250, Fellowship of Christian Athletes $150, International Club $100, Legion of Veterans Association $125, PHI BETA SIGMA FRATERNITY $350, S.O.T.A. $100, Students' Right to Life $125, TOPPERETTES $100, United Student Activists $125 (sums to $2,250). The entry gives the Topperettes $350 and buries Phi Beta Sigma in the $100-$150 group; it is the other way round. Also, the residual group's range is $100-$150 only if Phi Beta Sigma is excluded, which the corrected reading allows.

title: Dialogue Day puts administrators in Niteclass
body: President Donald Smith announced that 6 April 1994 would be Dialogue Day, when students could talk with administrators in Niteclass between noon and 2 p.m. The public relations committee handed out flyers for it alongside flyers for the coming election. It was one of a run of access events SGA staged that spring, with the memorial tree programme, the security phones due by 26 April and the campus clean-up.
note: REJECT as dated - announcement only. SGA minutes, 29 Mar 1994: "President Smith reported that April 6 is 'Dialogue Day'. Students can talk with administrators in Niteclass from 12 p.m. - 2 p.m." and, under PUBLIC RELATIONS, "Lena Sweeten-Garner passed out flyers concerning the upcoming election and Dialogue Day." So the announcement and the flyers are solid, but nothing shows the 6 April event happened or that anyone attended; an entry dated 1994-04-06 asserting it took place goes beyond the record. The supporting details are otherwise accurate - the same minutes give "Security phones should be in place by April 26" and the Memorial Tree programme.

title: SGA circulates flyers for a Jesse Jackson Jr. speech
body: Administrative vice president Scott Sivley passed out flyers at the 29 March 1994 congress meeting for Jesse Jackson Jr.'s speech on 18 April. The minutes record SGA distributing the publicity rather than booking the speaker, and name no fee or venue.
note: REJECT for an archive of events student government staged. SGA minutes, 29 Mar 1994, contain exactly one line: Administrative Vice-President Sivley "passed out flyers for Jesse Jackson, Jr.'s speech on April 18." That ties SGA to distributing publicity on 29 March and to nothing else - not to booking, funding, hosting or even attending, and the source gives no venue, sponsor or fee. It also does not establish that the 18 April speech occurred. The entry is commendably honest about all of this in its own body, which is why I would file it as a note against the 29 March meeting rather than as an SGA-staged speaker event dated 1994-04-18.

title: SGA moves to enter its own homecoming queen candidate
body: Congress voted in September 1994 to sponsor a candidate for homecoming queen, an idea the Herald put to a People Poll and drew an editorial cartoon about. The proposal set off a week of argument over whether student government belonged in a beauty pageant.

src.label: Herald 70:11, 22 Sep 1994 - Quarles, "Student Government Association to Enter Queen Candidate"

note: Headline verified: 'Quarles, Mitchell. Student Government Association to Enter Queen Candidate - Homecoming Queen', 22 Sep 1994. But the body's claim that the Herald 'put it to a People Poll and drew an editorial cartoon about' it is contradicted by the same issue: its People Poll is 'How Would Extended Alcohol Sales on Weekdays & Sunday Affect You?' and its editorial cartoon is 'Jimmy Carter Peace Delegation to Haiti'. 'A week of argument' is unsupported. Citation also mis-numbers the issue: the record is Vol. 70, No. 9, not 70:11.

title: President for a Day puts a student in Wetherby
body: SGA's President for a Day swap put student Nick Church in President Thomas Meredith's job for a day. The Herald carried paired pieces from Meredith and Church under the heading "Back to the ABCz."

src.label: Herald 70:35, 28 Feb 1995 - Grundy and Gagliardi, "Back to the ABCz - President for a Day"

note: The two articles exist ('Grundy, Julie. Back to the ABCz - President for a Day, Thomas Meredith' and 'Gagliardi, Melissa. Back to the ABCz - President for a Day, Nick Church', 28 Feb 1995), but neither is tied to student government. This archive tags SGA items explicitly - the clean-up item in the very same issue reads '- Student Government Association' - and these two carry no such tag. Nothing in the source calls it an SGA programme or mentions Wetherby.

title: Provide-A-Ride starts giving students rides home
body: SGA's Provide-A-Ride service began carrying students in January 1997. Within a week the Herald was warning that the programme needed more student support to survive.

src.label: Herald 72:29, 23 Jan 1997 - Batcheldor, "Student Government Association Gives Rides to Students"

note: The record confirms only 'Batcheldor, Matt. Student Government Association Gives Rides to Students', 23 Jan 1997. It does not name the service 'Provide-A-Ride', does not say the service began in January 1997, and contains nothing about the Herald warning a week later that the programme needed more student support to survive. Issue is Vol. 72, No. 31, not 72:29.

title: Designated driver cards go out to students
body: The designated driver cards SGA funded with $900 in November 1997 were distributed the day after this Herald report. The card entitled a designated driver to free soft drinks at participating restaurants instead of alcohol.

src.label: Herald 73:33, 17 Feb 1998 - Felkins, "Student Government Association's Designated Driver Cards Will Be Distributed Tomorrow"

note: Two independent problems. First, the money: the source is a Herald contents record whose only relevant line is 'Felkins, Melissa. Student Government Association's Designated Driver Cards Will Be Distributed Tomorrow - Drunk Driving, Alcohol'. It gives no $900 figure, nothing about November 1997 funding, and nothing about free soft drinks at participating restaurants. Second, the headline is an announcement of a future distribution, which the entry converts into a completed event. Issue is Vol. 73, No. 36, not 73:33.

title: Organizational Aid pays out $6,200 to 26 groups
body: Bill 98-9-F disbursed $6,200 to student organisations after two committee meetings totalling more than six hours. Awards ranged from $100 to the Residence Hall Association's $205, and reached groups from Free the Planet to the Jewish Student Organization.
note: The count is wrong. The bill lists 41 recipient organisations, not 26. Everything else checks out: '$6,200.00 budgeted for Organizational Aid'; 'over six hours in two different meetings'; Residence Hall Association $205 as the top award and $100 as the floor; Free the Planet and the Jewish Student Organization both present. Dated October 27, 1998.

title: Dialogue Day at Java City
body: SGA ran Dialogue Day on Tuesday 28 October 2003 from 12 to 2 p.m. at Java City near the library, giving students a chance to meet WKU administrators including their deans. It became a fixture SGA repeated in later years.

src.label: WKU SGA news page, 26 Oct 2003 (Wayback capture)

note: The cited page is a pre-event announcement, not a record of an event. Its 26 October 2003 item reads: 'Dialogue Day on Tuesday! Get a chance to meet WKU administrators, including your deans! It's on Tuesday at Java City (near the library) from 12:00 to 2:00.' The venue, hours and purpose all match, but nothing in the source shows the event took place, and 'It became a fixture SGA repeated in later years' is unsupported by this capture.

title: The autumn banquet closes the semester
body: SGA held its autumn banquet straight after the Congress meeting on 2 December 2003, the last meeting of the term, and had its yearbook photograph taken there. The calendar for the year also records a Parents' Weekend lunch on 20 September, a campus lighting and safety walk on 13 October, and forums on campus safety, plus-minus grading, academic issues, housing and elections.
note: The cited Events Calendar does not support the headline claim. Its December 2003 panel shows only '2 Congress Meeting 5:00 DUC 305' - no banquet, no yearbook photograph, and no indication this was the last meeting of the term. The calendar does support the second sentence: Parents' Weekend Lunch on 20 September, Campus Lighting/Safety Walk on 13 October, and forums on campus safety (11 Sep), plus/minus grading (9 Oct), academic issues (13 Nov), housing (12 Feb) and elections (11 Mar). A different, uncited SGA page (newsFall2003) does announce that 'The SGA banquet will be held right after the Congress meeting on Tuesday', but that is prospective and still says nothing about a yearbook photograph.

title: The spring banquet and the senior banquet
body: SGA's spring banquet was held on Tuesday 27 April 2004 from 5 to 8 p.m. in the Kentucky Building, in place of the usual Congress meeting. The senior banquet followed the next evening from 7.30 to 9 p.m. in the same building, business attire required.

src.label: WKU SGA news page, 20 Apr 2004 (Wayback capture)

note: The source is prospective, and it also conflicts with SGA's own calendar on the time. The cited 20 April 2004 news item reads: 'The Spring Banquet will be at the regular Congress meeting time, except it will be in the Kentucky Building. It is currently scheduled from 5:00 - 8:00 pm. The Senior Banquet will be next Wednesday from 7:30 - 9:00 pm in the Kentucky Building. Please dress in business attire.' Venue, hours, business attire and the day-after sequence all match, and the dates work out to 27 and 28 April - but 'currently scheduled' is an announcement, which the entry reports as an event that was held. Separately, SGA's own Events Calendar lists the 27 April banquet at 6:00 PM, not 5 to 8.

title: First Dine with the Decision Makers
body: SGA held the first Dine with the Decision Makers on 8 December 2009 from 4:30 to 6 p.m. in the Cupola Room of Downing University Center, where students discussed higher education with elected officials over dinner. President Kevin Smiley said 25 students had signed up through an online RSVP, the number capped by cost, and that five legislators and Bowling Green Mayor Elaine Walker would attend. The event grew out of a decision by the Board of Student Body Presidents that autumn that Kentucky's public universities should each mount student lobbying events.
money: attendance was capped because of the cost of the dinner

src.label: College Heights Herald 85:24, 8 Dec 2009 - "SGA to dine with lawmakers" (TopSCHOLAR)

note: The cited article is a same-day PREVIEW, not a report of a completed event: 'Students have a chance to interact with legislators... tonight'; 'The dinner is set to take place from 4:30 p.m. to 6:00 p.m.'; 'five legislators will attend'; '25 students are signed up to attend.' The entry converts this into 'SGA held the first Dine with the Decision Makers on 8 December 2009', which the source does not state. The word 'first' appears nowhere in the article, and nothing establishes it was the inaugural edition. The individual details (Cupola Room, RSVP cap due to cost, Mayor Elaine Walker, Board of Student Body Presidents' autumn decision on lobbying events, President Kevin Smiley) are all accurate to the source; only the 'held / first' framing fails.

title: Safety Walk found nearly thirty lights out
body: SGA held its annual Safety Walk on the evening of 26 October 2010, with Assistant Police Chief Mike Wallace and John Osborne, vice president for campus services and facilities, taking part. Executive vice president Kendrick Bryan reported that participants had found nearly 30 lights out around campus.

src.label: Herald, 10 Nov 2010 - "SGA invites regents to Dine with Decision Makers"

note: The cited 10 Nov 2010 article supports only the lights figure: 'Bryan said participants found nearly 30 lights that were out on campus at last week's campus safety walk.' It gives NO date - and 'last week's' relative to 10 November points to roughly 1-7 November, not 26 October. It also does not mention Mike Wallace or John Osborne at all. Those two names and the 26 October date come from the 19 Oct SGA-notes article, which said the walk 'will take place next Tuesday at 6 p.m.' with Wallace and Osborne 'helping out' - i.e. scheduled, not confirmed as attended. The entry needs re-sourcing or a corrected date.

title: Transcript voucher programme launched
body: On 28 February 2012 the senate allocated $1,225 for a transcript voucher programme, offering 175 free official transcripts, two per student, at a time when a transcript cost $7. Cory Dodds, SGA director of information technology and a bill author, said he hoped it would become an SGA staple like the free scantrons and blue books. Registrar Freida Eggleton worked with SGA on the rollout. The same meeting passed $500 for five $100 Study Away scholarships and $2,300 in Scholar Development and Study Abroad awards.
money: $1,225 for 175 vouchers; $500 in Study Away scholarships; $2,300 in grants

src.label: Herald, 29 Feb 2012 - "SGA to launch transcript voucher program"

note: The 29 Feb 2012 article supports the core allocation - 'The first bill passed at the SGA meeting Tuesday night allocated $1,225 for transcript vouchers... A total of 175 vouchers will be available with a limit of two per student' - plus '$500 from general senate funding... five $100 scholarships' and 'Additional $2,300 in funding for Scholar Development Grant Awards and Study Abroad Awards'. But three claims are absent from it: the $7 transcript price is never given (it is a division of 1,225 by 175, and appears only in a different, later article); Cory Dodds is not quoted or mentioned at all, so the 'SGA staple like the free scantrons and blue books' line is unsupported; and Registrar Freida Eggleton does not appear. Per the standard on amounts the source does not give, this fails.

title: Hidden Hacks of the Hill showed students what they were missing
body: WKU hosted Hidden Hacks of the Hill on 14 November 2017 in Downing Student Union, an SGA-funded event aimed at helping minority student groups find campus resources. The Writing Center, the Counseling and Testing Center and the WKU Food Pantry all tabled. Senator Divya Gangavelli spoke on the practical hacks, including how the White, Red and Purple bus lines could be used to get around campus and up the Hill.

src.label: Herald, 16 Nov 2017 - "Students learn the hidden hacks of the Hill"

note: The cited 16 Nov 2017 article credits the host as the university, not student government: 'WKU hosted Hidden Hacks of the Hill Tuesday, an event dedicated to helping minority student groups on campus familiarize themselves with on-campus resources.' It never says SGA funded or organised it - the sole SGA connection is that 'Student Government Association senator Divya Gangavelli took time to speak.' The words 'fund', 'bill' and '$200' do not appear. This is the pattern of a campus event not tied to SGA by the source. The funding claim is supported instead by the 1 Nov 2017 Herald piece, which reports Bill 20-17-F approving $200 for 'Hidden Hacks on the Hill' on 14 Nov. Everything else in the entry (Writing Center, Counseling and Testing Center, WKU Food Pantry tabling; Gangavelli on the White, Red and Purple lines and the Grise Hall route up the Hill) is accurate to the cited article.
